Oṃ! This is the sequence of the ritual for the great festival consisting of Śiva.
I bow to Mahāgaṇapati, the crest-jewel of the Āgamas, the son of Madanāri,
whose body is embraced by the arms of Vāmā, who sits firmly upon his lap.
I take refuge in the one born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, the bestower of desired boons upon those who seek him,
whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods headed by Brahmā.
He who is Śambhu himself, having come here from the ancient realm of Sadāśiva to bestow grace upon his devotees,
is renowned in this city of Kāñcī by the name Sadāśiva.
I bow to him who possesses gentle qualities and whose mind is free from the weight of evil teachers.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"Now, O Guha, I shall describe the procedure for the great festival of Maheśa,
beginning with the sacrifice of the bull and ending with the festival for the devotees, in due order."
First is the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga), second is the hoisting of the banner (dhvajāroha),
third is the large drum-beating (bṛhatāla), and fourth is the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
The worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālārcana*) is likewise [the sixth], followed by the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*);
the seventh is the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*), and then the eighth step.
Oṃ.
The sequence of the ritual for the great festival consists of the sacrifice to the Bull as the first part, and the hoisting of the banner as the second.
The third is the Bṛhattāla, and the fourth is the Aṅkurārpaṇa.
Next, the characteristics of the sacrificial hall according to the system of the Astra-yāga; seventh, the offering of the bali-oblation; and eighth, the sequence of the procession.
The ninth is the rite of encircling with light (pariveṣa), the tenth is the sequence of the eye-salve (nīrāñjana),
the eleventh is the auspicious thread (kautuka), and the twelfth is the collection of sacred fords (tīrthasaṃgraha).
On the thirteenth day there is the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), on the fourteenth the pilgrimage (tīrthaka),
on the fifteenth the descent (avaroha), and on the sixteenth the ceremonial bath (snapana) shall take place.
The marriage festival is considered the seventeenth, and beyond that is the festival of the eye-opening ceremony (*haktotsava*).

Having understood the festivals through such distinctions, the procedure for the most excellent nine-fold festival is prescribed according to the divisions beginning with the Śaiva and ending with the Daivika.
For example: in the first part of the night, one should begin the ritual observance (*adhivāsana*).

Therein, the preceptor and others—refraining from eating more than once, sleeping on the ground, anointing with oil, contact with women, and food provided by others—from the time of ascending [the seat] until the time of descending.

Free from food and other comforts, bathing at the three periods of the day, having first shaved his head and put on a new garment, he should perform the following practice after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and paying homage to his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
In that regard, the hoisting of the banner should be performed on the day before [the main rite], and the shaving of the head should be done.
On the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth,
seventh, eighth, and ninth days, the ritual offering (*bali*) should be performed twice each time.
On the day of the sacred ford (tīrtha), having offered the morning bali-oblation, one should begin (or perform) the full festival of the ford;
the nine-day festival, preceded by the hoisting of the banner, must be performed first.
The determination of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and so forth:
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it ends with Ārdrā; in Puṣya, it ends with Puṣya; in Māgha, it ends with Māghā; in Phālguna, it ends with Uttaraphalgunī; in Caitra, it ends with Citrā.
In Vaiśākha, until the end of Viśākhā; in Jyeṣṭha, until the end of Jyeṣṭhā or Mūla;
in Āṣāḍha, until the end of Uttarāṣāḍhā or Pūrvāṣāḍhā; in Śrāvaṇa, until the end of Śravaṇā; in Bhādrapada...
In Āśvina, [the asterism] ending with Pūrvabhādrapadā;

in Kārttika, ending with Aśvinī and likewise ending with Kṛttikā—such are the auspicious asterisms. On the full-moon day at the seashore, or at a river and so forth, when it is joined with the festival (parva), yet [the moon] is separated [from the asterism].

Or, one should have a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) constructed on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, or on the sixth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, or under a lunar mansion such as Deva-grāma and others, or under a lunar mansion desired by the patron (*yajamāna*).
In the ocean, it is at forenoon; in Puṣkara and other such places, at afternoon; in a river, at midday;
and at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), when the sun is in a lunar mansion suitable for village life, it is at evening.
One should observe the auspicious time (*tīrtha*).

When two constellations or two lunar days arrive within a single month, if the subsequent [constellation or day] is joined with a solstice (*viṣuvayana*), a transition (*saṃkrānti*), or other such astrological conjunctions (*yoga*), it should be observed as the preceding one.

One should begin the pilgrimage at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) during the month of Āśvina, or at best until the end of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), or until an eclipse; this is the rule for undertaking the pilgrimage.

During the Śivāditya festival, one should cause the raising of the banner at dawn on the day of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and at night on the morning [of the following day]; that is, the raising of the banner should be performed at evening on the first night and at dawn on the second day.
One should not place a banner upon a banner; rather, it must be so done.
The bull-bannered one;
if the banner of others is commenced, a great fault arises.
One should not perform a rite for personal welfare on a single plot of land, in a village, or during a festival for a deity; if it is performed, it results in harm to the king and the kingdom.
4) Prior to the commencement of the Vināyaka festival, having renovated everything from the mounts up to the chariot,
[one should prepare] the banana pillars for the area extending from the temple of the deity to the street.

Having decorated [the area] with betel-nut pillars, coconut trees, jackfruit trees, and so forth, as well as garlands of fruits, sprouts, and flowers appropriate for the season, along with mirrors, door-arches, canopies, banners, and rows of flags;
and having likewise decorated the water-stalls and rest pavilions, one should perform sweeping and the sprinkling of water.
Having caused the *nāḍī* [to be performed], one should cause the purification of the ground (*bhūśuddhi*) to be performed.
(p. 4) At the conclusion of the festival of Bhadrakālī, one should cause a festival for Vighneśvara to be held for nine days, seven days, three days, or one day.

Namely: having specially worshipped and adorned Vināyaka, Skanda, Vīraśāstā, the twenty-five forms of Skanda, Caṇḍeśa (or Caṇḍagaṇeśa), Śivāstra, Bhaktavigraha, and the others, preceded by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); and—
The preceptor, the officiating priest, the king, and the patron, together with Brāhmaṇas skilled in the three arts, at an auspicious moment, for the sake of the festival,
performed the worship of Mahādeva preceded by the worship of Vighneśvara.
Having had the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) recited with the appropriate mantras,
having performed the ritual bathing and worshipped Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa), having offered oblations ending with sweetmeats, edibles,
and foods, and having fed the Brahmins;
Having prayed, "May there be no obstacle," he should satisfy all those engaged in the work of the temple,
as well as the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless, with food and clothing; and [he should worship] Caṇḍeśvara, the king of weapons.
And having mounted Caṇḍeśvara, preceded by Vināyaka, upon a chariot or a palanquin and so forth,
accompanied by mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, and various banners, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, various foods, [various musical instruments], and the sound of Vedic chanting;
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should establish [the deity] in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa).
Then, the collection of wood should be performed, just like the collection of stone; thus one should carry out the collection of wood.

Having examined the tip or the root of one of these trees— such as the *bilva*, *khadira*, *devadāru*, *campaka*, *arjuna*, *aśoka*, *śirīṣa*, or *veṇu*— and having worshipped Śiva and offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should bind [the tree] and cut it with an axe.
One should cut [the line]. If it falls in the east, the north, or the northeast, it is auspicious; otherwise, one should abandon that site.
Having made it square, taking it along with the artisan, placing it upon a chariot and bringing it back,
bathing it with cow's products, tying the *kautuka* (protective thread) first, and again having the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness) recited,
one should place it in the bathing pavilion and rub it with fragrant oils and other substances for all [the deities].
One should cause betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there for the flagpole (dhvajadaṇḍa), one should place the pole in its center.
Having adorned [the deity] with garments and the like, having embellished [him] with garlands and so forth,
and having offered incense and lamps—
one should worship the three principles together with Īśvara, beginning from the portion of Śiva, in the square, octagonal, and circular sections.

Having worshipped him with the *praṇava* and raised him up (*praṇavenotthāpya*), one should place him in that location and consecrate him according to the procedure for general consecration (*sāmānyapratiṣṭhā*). Thus,
[one should install] the three pillars and three planks, either ending at the pinnacle (*sthūpyanta*), the crest (*cūlikānta*), or the gable (*śukanāsānta*).
One should have two handles made together with bells, joined with one hundred and eight tufts of *darbha* grass,
wrapped with a cord of *darbha*, and provided with rings; this is the procedure for the collection of wood and the installation of the staffs.
Regarding the collection of clay:
having collected clay from a riverbank or similar location as previously described,
one should proceed accompanied by the images of Vighneśvara and others, along with various musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas.
Having gathered the clay as previously described, and having had that clay carried by attendants, Māheśvara devotees, female attendants of Rudra (*rudragaṇikā*), elephants, and so forth,
around the city, he enters the temple.
Having placed the seedling on the altar, one should worship Vighneśa with *modakas* and other sweets,

cakes, and seasonal fruits such as stalks of sugarcane, coconut, wood-apple (*kapittha*), citron (*mātulaṅgaka*), banana, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), green gram (*mudga*), betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), and so forth.
Having offered [the earth] with all the ritual services (upacāra), one should worship it; such is the procedure for collecting the clay.
3. Regarding the sprouts (aṅkura): first is the flag-sprout (dhvajāṅkura), and second is the festival-sprout (utsavāṅkura).
One should perform the third, the "Sprout of the Tīrtha," as previously described.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the sprouts (2). Now follows the sacrifice of the bull (*vṛṣayāga*):
on the night preceding the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*), [the preliminary] consecration (*adhivāsana*)—

One should cause the ritual action to be performed. Then, having worshipped Śiva and made the formal request, and having adorned the site of the bull with canopies and other ornaments, the Guru, facing north, should stand.

Having assumed a steady posture as previously described, performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth, prepared the offering water (*arghya*), established it, worshipped the Lord of the Bull (*Vṛṣeśa*), and offered an oblation of mung-bean rice, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before him.
Having drawn a lotus in the center with a finger or similar object, having strewn it around with *kuśa* grass and flowers,
and having placed nine water-pots, one should worship the bull in the central pot preceded by the sixfold throne-rite, and [worship] the bull in the directions from the east to the northeast.
Homage to Gopati; homage to Śṛṅgin; homage to Nandin;
homage to Vṛṣapati; homage to Viṣāṇin; homage to Śaṅkukarṇa;
homage to Mahodara—thus [one performs] the placement of the seat and so forth with the root mantras.

Having worshipped— or rather, having fully honored the world-protectors— one should fashion the flag-cloth as previously described, nine cubits and so forth in length, with a width of one-fifth that length, and a tail equal to the width, with the tip of the tail being half of that.
One should take a fine and smooth piece of cotton or similar material for the head,

divide it into three parts, and having painted a bull in the middle part— or in one of the three parts— with that [white] substance, one should [paint] the horns, ears, and sprouts with yellow [pigment].
Having drawn two eyes, one white and one black, in front of that, and behind it a full water-pot, a lamp, a bell, a śrīvatsa, a svastika,
and other auspicious forms, he should commence the rite of the flag (dhvajayāga).
Alternatively, having spread out a cloth of the length of a staff and the width of a staff— as previously described— and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*),
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, and having worshipped the movable seat upon the bull, [one should perform the rite] in front of it.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and performed the fire oblation (*homa*) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual, and after the purification of the image (*beraśuddhi*), one should prepare two further sacrificial mounds elsewhere,
place [the image] in the center of a bull-cloth (*vṛṣapaṭa*), and [proceed] with a golden stylus (*hematūlikā*).
Having performed the opening of the eyes with the two mantras of the Sun and Moon, or with the Vṛṣa-gāyatrī:
"We know him who has sharp horns; we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas."
May that Bull inspire us.

(p. 8) Immediately after the opening of the eyes, having performed everything such as the showing of the cow and so forth, and having sprinkled [the image] with earth, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should bathe it with the products of the cow and other substances in a mirror and then perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*) in water.

k: 9) Having emerged from the water, one should bring the banner-cloth to the sacrificial hall; having sprinkled it again with cow-products and the like while reciting the *vṛṣagāyatrī*, and having placed it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship the sixfold throne (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) within the bull, preceded by meditation on its form.

He should form this intention. Then, having covered [the image] with a cloth, having performed the placement of the Brahma-mantras, having offered incense and lamps, having established the sleep-vessel (nidrākumbha), and having arranged the bulls and other figures around it.
One should perform worship.

Standing at the base of the bull, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-four principles (*tattva*), together with their presiding deities, from the crown of the head down to the feet.

Namely: having worshipped from "Obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva (sadāśivatattvāya namaḥ)" and "Obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding deity of the principle of Sadāśiva (sadāśivatattvādhipāya brahmaṇe namaḥ)," up to "Obeisance to the principle of Earth (pṛthivītattvāya namaḥ)" and "Obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha, the presiding deity of the principle of Earth (pṛthivītattvādhipāya śrīkaṇṭhāya namaḥ)."
Having envisioned [the area] as three sections and having offered a flower garland and a protective cord (*pratisara*), one should, as before, designate three portions.
In each portion, proceeding in order from the east and so forth:
"Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Ether"—these are the forms (*mūrti*).

Having assigned the presiding deities of the forms— Ukṣā, Gopati, Śṛṅgin, Nandin, Vṛṣapati, Viṣāṇin, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahodara— and having performed the *jīvanyāsa* with their respective root mantras, one should proceed with the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and other offerings.
Having worshipped with ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds, one should construct three enclosures on the outside.

Having supplicated the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), one should [offer] into the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. In the fire: [one should offer].
Having performed worship and offered three oblations, one should worship the Ātmatattva, Vidyātattva, and Śivatattva with the mantra "Oṃ,

salutations to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva," offering three oblations to each. Then, [one worships] the forms beginning with Earth (Kṣmāmūrti) with the mantra "Salutations to the lords of those [elements]."

Having thus worshipped and offered three oblations to each, and having offered one hundred or fifty oblations to each of the root-mantras and the Brahmāṅga-mantras, and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*,
the Guru, holding the *śāntikumbha* (peace-pitcher) in his hand, goes near the bull and performs the *śānti*.

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with water from the *kumbha* while reciting its root mantra, one should divide it into three parts using the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass; then, having touched them, recited the mantra, and offered oblations, one should conceal it with the *varma* mantra, seal it, and obtain the permission of the presiding deities of the *tattvas*.

Having caused [the mantra] to be heard, having deposited the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and having restrained it through fire-offerings (*homa*) or the sounding of the Vedas and so forth, or with great festivals of dance and song, one should perform this with devotion for at least one night.

Having offered the consecration of the bull (vṛṣādhivāsana), the directions, and the sacrificial oblation (bali), the preceptor should sleep as before; this is the procedure for the consecration of the bull.
2. The hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa):
On the following day, having performed the morning bath and other rites,

having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), having performed the ritual of the six limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should carry out the entire procedure for self-worship (*ātmapūjāvidhi*) as in the daily rite, and [then] the cloth-painting (*paṭa*).

Having worshipped the jars and other vessels in their proper order, and having likewise offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and sealed [the fire],
one should construct three mandalas in the pavilion and other areas, summon an attendant, and [protect him] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having sprinkled [the image] with water, put on the turban and upper garment, and lifted it up together with the cloth, the pitcher, and so forth— equipped with all musical instruments from the *astra* mantra to Caṇḍeśa amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums—

Having performed a circumambulation of the village accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures, and having entered the temple, he should place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) upon one cloth, the water-pot (kumbha) upon another, and [the remaining items] upon three sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila); then,

having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, [he should perform the rite] together with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka).
Having sprinkled the bull with water from the pitcher, having bathed it with jars of milk and other substances,

having adorned it with perfumes and the like, having offered sacrificial food such as chickpeas and so forth, and having likewise bathed the King of Weapons (the ritual sword) with water from that same pitcher, adorned it, and offered it, one should worship [it] until the conclusion of the recitation.

Having applied the powder of *rajanī* to the king of weapons (*astrarāja*) and having applied it himself, he should cause the powder of *rajanī* to be given to the kings, the devotees, the attendants, and everyone else; then,
having adorned the flagstaff with the *Śivagāyatrī*.
One should worship the bell.

Having mounted the deity upon a chariot or similar vehicle, with the trident at the very front and the preceptor behind it, the patron, together with all his devotees, [should proceed]. (p. 11) k: 12)

The city was equipped with all kinds of musical instruments, adorned with auspicious sprouts, and accompanied by full water-jars; it was joined with various types of parasols, fly-whisks, and lamps, and provided with processions and gifts; and in every direction and intermediate quarter, it was filled with singing, dancing, and the offering of oblations.

Having circumambulated [the temple] and entered the residence, one should bring [the image] to the place of the banner, recite the *puṇyāha* formula, sprinkle water upon the altar together with its pedestal, and worship [the deities] on the altar beginning from Śakti and ending with Śakti according to one's capacity.
One should meditate upon the flagstaff as having one foot, two arms, and three eyes; adorned with a line of hair,
a cord of *darbha* grass, and a white bodily form with a parrot-like nose, it is mounted upon a lotus seat.
The form of the staff.
Having meditated thus,
one should invoke Sadāśiva into the staff (daṇḍa), the triad of Śaktis into the staff-handle (yaṣṭi) and the board (phalaka),
the Sun and Moon into the secondary staff (upadaṇḍa), the presiding deity Takṣan into the cord (rajjū), and Vāyu into the cloth (paṭa).
Having worshipped the bull on the banner in due order, having offered green-gram rice or milk-rice to the bull,
having presented incense and lamps, and having given gold and other gifts to the Brahmins, [he should offer] the banner-cloth.
Having lifted [the image] with a rope and bound it, and having informed Śiva that the festival which was to be performed has now been completed, one should recite the *brahmatāla* verses;
then, for the purpose of dispelling obstacles, having offered an incalculable number of coconut offerings (*nālikera-bali*), at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*)...
Accompanied by various musical instruments, the preceptor stands at the base of the staff;

having sprinkled it with *arghya* water and having first touched it himself, he should quickly raise it together with the image-makers (*mūrtipas*), who have been appointed as attendants by means of the *arghya*.
Having wrapped it with a rope in a clockwise direction, one should tie it at the base of the staff.
From that point until the conclusion of the ritual bathing (tīrtha), one should [attend to] the bull three times or twice a day.

One should perform worship. Afterwards, having gone to the vicinity of the water-pot (*kumbha*)— or, according to some manuscripts, the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)— and having offered the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta*), one should dismiss the fire of the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*).

Pure dancing should be performed in the cardinal and intermediate directions; this is the procedure for hoisting the banner. Regarding the measurement of the sacrificial balls (*balipiṇḍa*), the measurement for the coconut is twenty-five balls.
By means of the staff-seat [the ritual] becomes pure;
O Śikhidhvaja, a woman without a son who consumes that drop (*bindu*) shall obtain a son; it destroys disease, removes all defects, and is the essence of virility.

k: 14) The Raising of the Banner (and its fruit): In whatever kingdom this installation of the banner-pole is performed, there is no untimely death therein, nor is there misfortune, even among evildoers.
There, there is no fear of approaching [the object], no obscuration, and no confusion;
nor do erroneous cognitions generally arise even for yogins.
The rain-cloud pours forth at its proper time; there is abundance of food and the king is victorious.
All beings are peaceful, and the milk-yielding cows overflow with milk.

An ungrateful person, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a killer of a cow, attains liberation from sin upon merely seeing a traveler’s lodging; how much more so for one who actually performs the act of hospitality for the three generations of his family!
When the raising of the great banner (*mahādhvajāroha*) is performed, the fruit is multiplied ten million times.
3. The ritual procedure for the *bherī* (drum) and *brahmatāla*.
It has been stated in the *Utsavapaddhati* that for the sake of pleasing all the gods,
the drum (*bherī*) is struck at the conclusion of the evening protection ritual (*sāyarakṣā*).
One should commence the rite of invoking the deity either before an image of the god or at the top of a banner.

Having prepared three sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) there, one should place a trident on the first, a cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in front of it, and a drum (*bherī*) in front of that; to the south, one should set down a nose-staff (*ghoṇadaṇḍa*).
(Then one should perform the ritual placement [nyāsa] of the principles, worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, powers, and so forth upon the trident.
For example: on the central petal, "Obeisance to Śivatattva."
Salutation to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-tattva; on the left petal: salutation to the Vidyā-tattva;
salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the Vidyā-tattva; on the right petal: salutation to the Ātman-tattva; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the Ātman-tattva; on the back [of the leaf]...

Salutation to Pārvatī on the [front] part; salutation to Senānī on the region of the pitcher (kumbha); salutation to Vighnarāja on its mouth; salutation to Madana on the tip of the staff; salutation to Bhāskara on the base of the staff;
and salutation to Caṇḍeśvara at the base of the staff, starting from the southeast (āgneya).
On the seven petals: salutation to Brāhmī; salutation to Māheśvarī; salutation to Kaumārī;
salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; salutation to Vārāhī; salutation to Māhendrī; salutation to Cāmuṇḍā; in the middle of the western petal, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā.
In the center of the circle of Kubera, [one says] "Obeisance to Kātyāyanī. At the base of the trident,
one should invoke the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus,
the deities of the Aśvins, and the eighteen Gaṇas.
Having invoked the deities, worshipped them, summoned them, and pronounced the remaining benedictions,
one should strike the drum. Then, having wrapped the drum with a variegated cloth, one should proceed.

In the center, one should worship Rudra; in the seven stakes, the Mothers; and in the nine pegs, the Planets. In the cords, Vāsukī; and in the blow, Ṣaṇmukha—having worshipped them in this sequence and adorned them with perfumes and other offerings.
One should strike the drum.
Having meditated upon the preceptor as the weapon in the form of a drop (bindu), one should strike it three times with *darbha* grass.
If that sound reaches the path of the ears of living beings, they become cleansed of sin.
Afterwards, having summoned the musicians, [he provides] the sacrificial thread and the upper garment.

Having taken perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having placed a flower in his hand, he too, with the permission of the Ācārya, should cast the flower upon the drum, place the musical instrument upon his shoulder, and strike it with the *nanditāla* rhythm.

Then, having summoned Śiva and all the other gods, the eighteen classes [of attendants], Indra and the other guardians of the directions, the oceans, the mountains, the islands, and all the netherworlds, he should cause them to hear [the proclamation].

Then, for the purpose of invoking the deities beginning with Madhya, one should perform the invocation of the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), Soma, Skanda, the Goddess, Vināyaka, Skanda, Nandin, Caṇḍa, Bhaktavigraha, and others, together with all the auspicious ones; having taken recourse to the station of the Bull and offered the worship and oblation, one should perform the dance.

Having attained satisfaction through song, wind-instruments, and so forth, and having resorted to the station of Brahmā, one should perform all the rites such as the *puṇyāha* proclamation and sprinkling within that mandala; then, having meditated upon and fully worshipped [the deity],
and having offered a *bali* for the sake of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should thereafter [employ] the rhythm (*tāla*) of Brahmā and the musical mode (*rāga*).

Having gratified [the deity] with the vaṅkula dance, the *samapāda* posture, the *pañcama* rhythm, the *gucchapuṭa* instrumental music, and so forth, one should thereafter take recourse to the direction of Indra;
having performed the rites from the seat (*āsana*) up to the offering (*bali*) within that mandala as before, [one should perform] the *tāla*.

Having performed the *samatāla* dance, the *bhujaṅga* hand gesture, and the *kaumeśī* instrumental music, and having likewise performed the *paṭa* [dance], one should perform the worship of Agni and so forth, up to the offering (*bali*), in the southeastern direction; then,
with the *varāṭī* melody and *mattā* rhythm, one should perform the *varaṇa* dance and the *maṇḍala* hand gesture.

Having gratified [the deity] with the *kollivādya*, *udghaṭita*, and other [musical pieces], and having performed the rites for Yama in the southern direction— from worship up to the offering of bali— one should perform the *vāga* dance, the *rāmagiri* rhythm, the *bhṛṅgiṇītāla* rhythm, the *daṇḍapāda* dance, and the *kauśika* instrumental music.

Having gratified [the deities] with "militamaṭṭayaṃ" and other [mantras], and having offered worship and bali to Nirṛti in the southwest (nairṛta), one should perform the dance of Rāga, the Bhairavī rhythm, the Mallatāla rhythm, the Bhujaṅgatrāsa dance, the Paṇ-naṭṭa dialect, instrumental music, the Lambaka, and so forth.
In the western quarter, having offered an oblation to Varuṇa as before, one should perform the dance known as Rāga, Kuñjarī, Nāgatāla, Ākuñcika, Paṇ, Śrīkāmara,
and the instrumental music known as Siṃhanāda; then, in the northwestern quarter, [one should offer] an oblation to Vāyu as before.
Having offered the *rāga*, the *deśāgiri* rhythm, the *tāla* rhythm, the dance performed by the serpent,

and the musical instrument for the nine-headed one (*navakeśi*), and having made the utterance "jampaṭam," one should meditate on Kubera in the north as before, offer the *bali*, and [offer] the *rāga*.

Having satisfied [the deity] with the Gauḍhika rhythm, the Gaulitāla rhythm, the Ākuñcita dance, the Kauśika instrumental music, and the Pañcama [note], one should meditate upon Īśāna in the northeast as before,
worship him, offer the bali, and [employ] the Tuṇḍīra melody and rhythm.

Having gratified [the deities] with the ḍhakkarī dance, the *ūrdhvapāda* [dance], the hand-drum (*paṇava*), the *śālāpāṇi*, the *kumbhavādya*, and so forth, and having circumambulated [the shrine] clockwise in succession by Indra and the others, one enters the temple and [raises] the banner (*dhvaja*).
"One should offer the special oblation at the base or on the pedestal of the offering" is the rule for the Great Tāla (or Brahma-tāla).
5. The Procedure for the Worship of the Sacrificial Hall:
Then, having performed the auspicious sprouting rite (*maṅgalāṅkura*) according to the previously mentioned method,
Immediately thereafter (or, according to *k*: immediately after the completion), the worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) is performed.

In front of the deity, or in the northeast, southeast, north, or west, having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) measuring five cubits or more with its door facing west, one should [proceed] in its center.

As previously stated, the altar (vedikā), together with its secondary altar (upavedikā), should be made like the surface of a mirror. Outside of that, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east and ending in the northeast should be arranged in sequence as the bases:
the half-moon, the triangle, the circle, and the hexagon.
The lotus-shaped and eight-cornered sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas): between Candra and Īśāna (or Indra), there is either a circle or a square;
alternatively, according to the five-fold system, the circle is primary in the northeast, with [the others] in the four directions.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are square.
Alternatively, having made one [pit] circular or square and having smeared it with cow-dung, [one should prepare] a canopy, a banner, and an umbrella.
The door-arch of the gateway, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and the eight auspicious signs—
namely, the mirror, the full water-jar, the bull,
the pair of chowries, the *śrīvatsa*, the *svastika*, the conch, and the lamp— constitutes the eight divine auspicious emblems (*devāṣṭamaṅgala*).
The *sruk* [ladle] is endowed with the ten weapons: the vajra, the *śakti*, the staff (*daṇḍa*), the sword, the noose,
as well as the goad, the banner, the mace, the trident, and the lotus-wheel.

Having constructed [the sacrificial hall] equipped with the collection of implements such as the bellows and so forth, one should initiate the festival at the time of sunset; this is the rule for the characteristics of the sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā-lakṣaṇa-vidhi).

6 – The Ritual Procedure for the Weapon-Sacrifice (Astrayāga). The Preceptor, together with the officiating priests, having performed the evening twilight worship and the special twilight worship, enters the temple and prepares a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the deity.
Having consecrated with the Astra-mantra and sprinkled water over new, very smooth, and very sturdy jars—
ranging from those made of gold down to those of clay— free from blemish, provided with tufts of grass, covered with lids, and accompanied by cloth, fruit, and sprouts;
Having washed with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra those [images] which are accompanied by sūtras and endowed with gold, jewels, and so forth, possessing the characteristics as described;
having fumigated them and filled them with scented water using the *hṛdaya* mantra, [one should place them] upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

Having placed the *śivakumbha* in the center, the *vardhanī* to the north, and the eight *ghaṭas* around them, one should consecrate the *kumbha* with the *mūrti-mantra* and the *vardhanī* with the *śakti*,
[and worship] from Ananta up to Śikhaṇḍin.

Having worshipped the [deities] ending with Śikhaṇḍin within the jars, and having likewise worshipped the weapons beginning with Nandi and ending with [the final weapon] around them, one should summon the attendants,
hold the Śiva-jar and the Vardhanī in sequence, and [worship] from the Vajra up to the Cakra.
Having circumambulated the celestial chariot with the sounds of conchs and drums, as well as the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures, and having led it into the sacrificial hall,
[one should place] eight *droṇas* of rice together with *darbha* grass in the center of the altar.

Having strewn [the area] with rice, half that amount of sesame and parched grain, and seven types of grains, and having placed the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*), the *vardhanī*, and the pitchers of the Vidyēśvaras in their midst, one should establish [the deities] beginning with Dharma and ending with Sūrya in their respective places, accompanied by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Together with the patrons (*yajamāna*), the preceptor (*guru*)— preceded by the worship of Vināyaka— should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made; having performed the worship of the Sun (*saura-pūjā*) as usual and having dismissed [the deity], he should perform ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), effect the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and [prepare] the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*).
Having prepared the general *arghya* and worshipped the gates starting from the east,
one should worship two [deities] at each gate— beginning with Nandin and ending with Caṇḍa— as before; then, having propitiated the gatekeepers in the west as usual.
Having worshipped Vāstunātha in the southwest, and having seated [the disciple] to the south of the Brahma-position, facing east,
one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, as well as the special *arghya* offering, and [worship] oneself.

Having performed the self-protection (*ātāna*), having adorned [the site] together with the image-bearers (*mūrtipāḥ*) using perfumes and other offerings up to the *uṣṇīṣa*, and having duly prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should perform the purification of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the water of the *pañcagavya* offering.
Having worshipped the Śiva-kumbha and Vardhinī as before up to the end of the recitation (*japa*),
one should meditate upon the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) together with their vehicles and weapons, worship them,
and then honor Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*).
One should cause all [the participants] to hear the command of Śiva.

Then, having sat down to the south of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship the seat for the jar of Śiva (śivakumbha), beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti; [then perform] the breaking of the staff (daṇḍabhaṅgī) and the breaking of the head (muṇḍabhaṅgī).
Having placed the Śiva-mantra endowed with all the paths along with the artistic arrangement of its parts (*kalābhaṅgī*) as previously described,
and having meditated upon and invoked Him, one should perform the *śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa* upon the *vardhanī* vessel.
The meditation on the Goddess: She has two arms, a beautiful face, lovely breasts, and is in the full bloom of youth;
she wears fine silk garments, is peaceful, and her face is slightly pale like that of Brahmā.
(The Laughing One)
One should meditate upon the Goddess, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a throne like Hara, and wearing a crown and a casket, according to the prescribed sequence.

Having meditated, having invoked them by means of their root-mantra, and having worshipped those two with the fivefold enclosure and the five offerings, having presented the food offering and the recitation, having offered into the fire, and having prayed, [one should worship] in the corners starting from the southeast.
Having worshipped the Dharma and the other [deities] and having caused the command of Śiva to be heard, they should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the *kuṇḍa* and ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should divide the fire into nine or five parts and deposit it into the *kuṇḍas* (or *kumbhas*) starting from the east; then, having worshipped each respective Śiva along with his limbs (*aṅgas*), [one performs] the offering of *caru* and the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) as ancillary acts...
Together with the image-worshippers (*mūrtipaiḥ*), they should perform the oblation; having specifically worshipped Śiva in each of those respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍeṣu*)—
[offering] sacrificial fuel-sticks (*yajñasamidhaḥ*).
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees are in the directions starting from the east;
and the Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees are in the corners starting from the southeast.

With the principal [oblation], *palāśa* wood should be used, and that is approved everywhere. Having offered *caru*, parched grain (*lāja*), mustard, barley, sesame, green gram (*mudga*), black gram (*māṣa*), *śimbā*, *āḍhaka*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and horse gram (*kulattha*), and having offered at the end of the substances with the *vyāhṛti* mantras;
They should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or one thousand, or five hundred, together with the *pūrṇāhuti*,
using the root mantra. Then, having performed the salutation to the fire with sandalwood paste and other offerings, [they should proceed].
Having performed the protection rite for the fire-oblation and having caused the primary liṅga and the other images to be offered,
he himself, together with the officiating priests,
takes up the trident and, having brought it there to the northeast or the northwest, installs it.
One should perform this very rite every day, both evening and morning.
Thus ends the procedure for the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*).
11. The procedure for binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*).

Then, from gold, silver, or cotton, one should prepare a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) made of any one of these materials; it should consist of nine fierce lunar days (*tithi*), measure sixteen finger-breadths in length, and be equal in thickness to the *liṅga* or to its stalk (*nāla*) when placed upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
Having filled a small vessel with rice, parched grain, and flowers, and having drawn a lotus in its center, one should place upon it ashes,
turmeric, dūrvā grass, fragrant substances, flowers, fruits, and gold.

Having offered betel and other items, having cleansed that thread with *tryambaka* ashes, having caused the proclamation of a "holy day" (*puṇyāha*), having worshipped it preceded by the sixfold rising from the seat, having offered incense and lamps, and having circumambulated the temple, one enters within and [worships] Śiva.

Having worshipped him and offered incense and lamps, one should meditate upon Vāsuki at the base of the *liṅga*, hold it there with the root mantra, bind it to the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) at the navel-region with its own root mantra, offer ashes with the *Tryambaka* mantra, and [place] upon that—
Having offered the *rajanī* [powder] and worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should bind it to the central petal of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).

Then, for the *beras*, one should bind [the mantra] from the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) up to the Food-offering (*bhakta*) on the right hand, using the *tryambaka* [mantra] together with the Heart-mantra (*sahṛd*).
For the female images such as Gaurī and others, one should bind the *kautuka* (protective thread) on the left hand using the root-mantra of Gaurī;
and for oneself, the officiating priests, the bearer of the sacrificial offerings, and the striker of the drum (*bherī*).

Having tied the *kautuka* (sacred thread) for the ten weapons and having placed ashes and turmeric powder upon it, one should fix the *kautuka* onto the middle of the flagpole and bind it very firmly with the turmeric along with flowers at the knots (*granthi*).
One should cause all [the participants] to receive powdered saffron, gold-leaf, betel, and so forth;
this is the procedure for the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana). 7. The Procedure for the Offering of Sacrificial Oblations (balidāna).

Then, during the great festival, Bali should offer the oblation either from the station of Brahmā to the end of the banner at morning and evening, or from the bull to the end of the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*).

For example: in locations such as the Brahma-sthāna and others, there should be a single pedestal for each, measuring one cubit in width and length, half that in width [for the next], and eight or twelve finger-breadths in thickness, provided with three girdles.
Having constructed pedestals made of stone endowed with a pericarp and eight petals,
or else made of brick or solid wood, possessing the proper characteristics,
and having smeared them with five powders according to their respective directions;
Having cooked either a full *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of rice, and having taken it into the vessel for the offering (*balipātra*), one should sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*. Then,
having brought half of that other [portion] into a cooking pot, [one should prepare] the food-sign (*annaliṅga*).

One should fashion it with the proper characteristics; having prepared that [image], twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in girth, together with its pedestal, and having smeared it with curd;
Having duly established the meditation—
the Pāśupata meditation—
one [should meditate on] the three-eyed, four-armed deity wearing a crown of matted hair.
With his right hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a rosary in his left hand.
On the right [side], he is joined with a trident, endowed with a fierce gaze,
adorned with serpent ornaments, and has hair standing upright above and hanging down below.
One should worship this divine Pāśupata [mantra] in the center of the *liṅga*.
Alternatively— having worshipped Śiva as before— the Preceptor, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
accompanied by the king of weapons consisting of the ten missiles, and [endowed] with everything from the sacred ash (*bhasman*) up to the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*)...
Adorned with ashes, an uṣṇīṣa, and other ornaments, accompanied by attendants (*paricāra*;

*k*: accompanied by followers), together with various banners, parasols, chowries, and the like, amidst the sounds of diverse musical instruments, bells, and the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), and accompanied by dancers and singers.
One should offer the *bali* together with a singer.
Regarding the specific deities of the *bali* for the nine-day festival, they are stated in order as follows:
on the first day, "To Vighnarāja, svāhā"; on the second, "To the Bhūtas."
Svāhā!—in the third [offering], svāhā to the Ṛṣis; in the fourth, svāhā to Indra;
in the fifth, svāhā to Brahmā; in the sixth, svāhā to Viṣṇu; in the seventh, svāhā to Rudra; in the eighth, svāhā to Īśvara; in the ninth.
"Sadāśivāya svāhā"— on these days, the oblation (havir) should be offered at the conclusion of the linga worship;
[it consists of] pure rice mixed with clarified butter and soaked in curd.
One should cast [the offering] the size of a hen’s egg;
this is the special bali. To Rudra Kumbhodara at the cow-pen, to Laṅkā upon the kuśa grass, and to the rivers in the [water].
To Gaṅgā at the pond, to Kṣetramūrti in the assembly hall, to Sarasvatī, to Durgā,
to Mahālakṣmī in the treasury, and to Bhīma at the gate— thus, with "Svāhā," one should offer the bali offering in the evening and in the morning.

One should assign [the offerings]. Having entered the courtyard (ālyam) from the station of Brahmā down to the pedestal for the offering (balipīṭha), or as far as the staff (daṇḍa), one should cast the remainder upon the pedestal for the offering.
Having discarded the food offering into water, washed one's feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*),
and smeared oneself with pure ashes, one should enter; this is the rule for the measurement of the *bali* offering.

8. The procedure for the procession (*yānakrama*) is as previously described; having adorned the processional paths (*vīthī*), [one should place] various ornaments and flowers upon a chariot, a stage, a palanquin, a litter (*śibikā*), or similar vehicle.
Having brought the deity endowed with radiance together with Śakti to the root-seat (mūlasthāna),
having invoked him, offered incense and lamps, and worshipped him with a handful of flowers,
[one should worship] the form (bera) together with the sequence beginning with Śakti and ending with Bhakta.
One should proceed in a clockwise direction.

In front [of the image], accompanied by various ornaments and musical instruments such as kettledrums (bherī), one should place the Śailādī and others; within that interval, Nandī and Vināyaka, and in the middle, Subrahmaṇya, along with the Goddess.

The preceptor, standing to the left side, should first [install] Soma and Skanda, then the clay images (bhaktabera) either in front or behind, and after that Caṇḍeśvara; then he should recite the Mūla-mantra or the Aghora-mantra an unlimited number of times.
On the left side is the king; behind him are the servants;

in front of the deity are dancers, genealogists, singers, and drummers; on both sides are those engaged in dance, along with the Rudra-prostitutes; in front are the great Śaivas; and behind are those accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures.
Thereafter, those born of the four castes who follow the Māheśvaras obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Having thus gratified the God, on the morning of the first day, [one should perform] the *aṅga*... (k)
On the first night, a lion;

on the second day, the Sūryasoma yantra; on the third night, the Bhūta yantra; on the fourth, a haṃsa; on the fifth night, a nāga; and on the sixth night, a bull. Between the circumambulations, the food should be served.
One should perform the serving (*pariveṣaṇa*).
For example: in a courtyard (*poṅkaṇa*) of gardens and the like... [k: in gardens and so forth].

At every step, having gratified the Lord with offerings such as fruits and with betel leaves and other items, accompanied by the Vedas as the praise, the Śruti as the lute, the Veda as the flute-singer, the Upaniṣads as the dancer, and the Purāṇas as the courtesan of Rudra, one should cause Him to enter the temple.
On the fifth day, at night, having placed the Āndolikā together with the Śikhara upon the Rāvaṇa-machine, or on the sixth day, having placed it in a palanquin or on a litter,
one should perform the Cūrṇotsava as described below, [using] saffron and musumbha.

Having sprinkled the deities with water from safflower, turmeric, and other substances, and having smeared all the deities with saffron paste, one should sprinkle them again. On the seventh [day], at night, [one should worship] the deity mounted upon an elephant; on the eighth, [one should worship] the chariot under the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) at night.

In the morning, having performed the evening ritual at night, they mount their horses; at the time of departure, they are mounted on horses, equipped with weapons such as spears, and provided with bows and shields.

The attendants of Rudra, adorned with all ornaments, should walk around [the site]. In the meantime, having suppressed the wicked and protected the virtuous, and having caused [them] to hear all matters of dharma and adharma, he should lead them into the abode.
On the ninth day, one should ride in a palanquin yoked to a human-powered machine along with a cart; on the tenth day at night, [one should apply] black ointment.

Having placed the deity upon a jeweled lion-throne (*ratnasiṃhāsana*) or a basket (*śimbikā*), and having circumambulated the city and other sites, one should carry the consecrated food around the top of the palace and the top of a flagstaff, and then cast it at a crossroads.
Immediately thereafter, the preceptor should have the rite of *nīrāñjana* performed by married women or the attendants of Rudra.
Then, having offered a water-pot lamp (*ghaṭadīpa*) to the deity at the front of the gate or atop the banner,

Immediately thereafter, the Rudra-prostitute, carrying a night-lamp along with a water-pot and holding collyrium in her hands, having performed circumambulations in due order accompanied by dancing, singing, and all types of musical instruments, [worships] Śailādi, Nandin, Vināyaka, Skanda, and the Goddess.
Together with the devotees of Caṇḍeśvara, they should circumambulate [the deity] in the morning and proceed to the temple.
Then, accompanied by those singing auspicious songs and all musical instruments, having caused Somāskanda to enter the temple, [they should proceed] to the pavilion for the installation and so forth.
Having established [the deity] in its proper place, having drawn the curtain, having offered the great oblation,
and having worshipped with all ritual services, one should offer coconuts, sugarcane juice, mung beans, and fruits appropriate for that season, in order to remove fatigue.
Having adorned the Brahmins with perfumes and flowers, one should feed them;
one should feed the devotees of Śiva and the most destitute without hesitation.
Alternatively, one may perform the vehicle (*yāna*) in another manner; this is the ritual procedure for the sequence of vehicles.
10. The Ritual Procedure for the Eye-Salve (*nīrāñjana*).

For the purpose of the *nīrājana* rite, having taken five vessels made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or other materials— each one span (*vitasti*) in width and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in height— and having placed them upon the mandala, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the fire-seed syllable (*agnibīja*) and the Brahma-mantras.

Having consecrated it with the four ritual actions (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*), and having displayed the *śūla-mudrā* and the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should take a lamp together with vessels containing ghee and auspicious verses (*svasti-sūkta*) that proclaim blessings, place it upon the head, and—

Having performed a circumambulation of the village and having placed [the image] upon a mandala (or pavilion) before the deity, one should rotate it three times each from the head down to the feet with the *brahma-mantras*, [offering] a mirror, umbrella, chowries, fan, ashes, and so forth.
Having offered the ashes and so forth, and having presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the root mantra,

one should prostrate; then, after having the [deity] carried by the attendants (*gaṇikā*) as before, one should cast [the deity] onto the pedestal (*pīṭha*) or onto the bull (*vṛṣa*), accompanied by the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, along with musical instruments (*vādya*).
Having performed the washing of the feet and other preliminary rites, one should enter the abode; this is the procedure for the *nīrāñjana* rite.
12. The procedure for the collection of sacred waters (*tīrtha*).
On the day prior to the *tīrtha*, one should collect the materials for the *tīrtha*.

Having performed the protection (*rakṣā*) as before and caused the benedictions (*āśis*) to be recited, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the middle of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) as previously described.
Having placed that jar which causes the state beyond the mind (manonmanī) in the center of the eight surrounding jars,
[one should worship] her who has the luster of vermilion, possesses three eyes, and bears the digit of the nectar-moon.
She wears a crest-ornament and red garments; she is bent by the weight of her full, high, and swelling breasts, and is rich with the onset of youth.

The Goddess, the source of the universe, adorned with various ornaments, residing in a lotus, her form transferred into the seed-syllable, endowed with the noose and goad, and granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons.
I pay homage.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one should offer oblations] into the eight jars starting from the east with: *namaḥ gaṅgāyai* (salutation to Gaṅgā), *namaḥ yamunāyai* (salutation to Yamunā), *namaḥ narmadāyai* (salutation to Narmadā),
*namaḥ sarasvatyai* (salutation to Sarasvatī), *namaḥ sindhave* (salutation to Sindhu), *namaḥ godāvaryai* (salutation to Godāvarī).

Having worshipped with all the ritual services (*upacāra*), beginning with the invocation, using "Salutation to Kāverī! Salutation to Tāmraparṇī!", and having caused [the image] to be borne on the head,
one should [place it] equipped with the *astra-mantra* and joined with all musical instruments (*sarvātodya*) on this day.

Having circumambulated the city, one should direct [the practitioner] toward bathing places such as rivers for the purpose of ritual ablution; this is the procedure for the collection of sacred sites (*tīrthasaṃgrahaṇavidhi*).
13. The Ritual for the Powder Festival (Cūrṇotsavavidhi).
On the days following the day of the collection of sacred substances (tīrthasaṃgraha), one should begin the powder [festival] after the offering of the bali oblation.

k: 32) Having drawn two lotuses on a double sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) at the top of the palace, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having strewn it with *darbha* grass, one should place a trident upon one [mound] and [make] a mortar and pestle from trees such as the *plakṣa*,
*udumbara*, *aśvattha*, or *paṭa*, and [the pestle] from *khadira*.

Having marked it with the characteristic signs, having established it by others, having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*),
one should wrap both the mortar and the pestle with a cloth.
Having encircled [the area] with the mantra "brahmadaivatyam," one should worship the eight jars of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) surrounding the *rudrakumbha* between the two mortars;
or alternatively, having worshipped Śiva, one should worship [the jars] surrounding the mortar.
Having placed dūrvā grass, sahadevī, koṣṭha, turmeric, oil-seeds, betel leaf, fragrant flowers, and ashes upon the petals starting from the east,
and having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*), one should [place] the Earth in the mortar and the Mace-bearer (*musala*) in the pestle.

Having worshipped Meru and placed it in that mortar— with either the *pada-mantra* or a hymn of praise— and having ground it into powder with blows from the pestle by means of courtesans, one should [mix] that powder at night with oil, ghee, and the water known as *gandhodaka*.

Having mixed it with gold, the preceptor takes that powder, places it in vessels, consecrates it, and causes it to be applied along with ashes to the primary *liṅga*; then, having donned a turban of saffron and smeared it with that paste—
Having offered incense and lamps, having applied *cūrṇa* to all the *beras*, and having smeared them with that paste— or not—
having displayed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*) and having applied it oneself, [one does so] for all of them.
Having offered the uṣṇīṣa, myrobalan fruit, betel leaf, and so forth, and having circumambulated the city and other sites together with the trident, one should cause [the deity] to enter the temple.
Alternatively, having established the weapon-vessel (astrakumbha) and the vajra-vessels and so forth—
"One should worship"— this concludes the ritual procedure for the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
Afterwards, having performed the rite of sprouts (*aṅkura*) as before, one should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrthasnāna*).

14— Bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrthasnāna*). For the purpose of removing the defect of being touched by those who are untouchable, for the attainment of the grace of the sacred ford, for bringing about what is dear to all the gods, and for the attainment of the fruits of dharma and other goals.

For the sake of accomplishment (*siddhyartham*), for the purpose of attaining the state of *Sālokya* and other [liberations], at the bank of a sacred ford (*tīrthatīre*), together with one’s power (*śakti*), accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments and praises, along with the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), Soma, Skanda, and others, as well as sprouts (*aṅkura*), parasols (*chatra*), chowries (*cāmara*), and so forth.
Having established the deities before that [altar], together with the *tīrtha* pitchers and the prepared *prapādika* [water-offering],
one should descend upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of them— placing Manonmanī in the center and the eight pitchers of the Gaṅgā and others— along with the *pālikā*s.
Having specially established [the deity] and worshipped [him], one should invoke Durgā in the northeast,
as well as the thirty-three deities and the eighteen Gaṇas in the vicinity of the trident.

Having performed the invocation of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and having released the protective amulets (*kautuka*) of the deities— such as those with weapons and so forth— by casting them into the middle of the sacred bathing site (*tīrtha*),
one should consecrate [the disciple] with the respective jars, beginning with Śiva and ending with the Weapon (*astra*), together with the protective cords (*pālika*).
He should perform the ritual bath together with all the people. Then the preceptor, having bid farewell to the deities of the sacred site (tīrtha), enters the temple and,
having consecrated each respective water-pot (kumbha) for all the deities, [offers] the food offering (naivedya).

Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, and having entered the temple, all those present in their respective places, accompanied by the chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa*, place unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*); then the instructor (*deśika*), preceded by a blessing, [dismisses them] to their respective places with those unbroken rice grains.
"One should cause [him] to enter"—this is the procedure for bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
(p. 28) Now follows the procedure for the ritual bath with a jar (*ghaṭasnāna*):
O God, for the sake of the festival powder for Hara and for the sake of establishing order among the people...
For the sake of attaining grace and for the sake of attaining proximity to deities such as Indra,
one should perform the ritual bathing of the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*).
Having performed the special fire-oblation (*viśeṣahoma*) in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), [one should do so] especially in those pits.

They should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblations (as before). Having joined each respective Lord with the Principal [deity] and having worshipped Śiva, they should again offer a *pūrṇāhuti*, and then worship the Śiva-pitcher and other vessels with special care.
Having combined the incense and lamps and offered them, having given the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others,
and having given garments, gold, and so forth to the attendants and others, one should lift the jars as before, circumambulate the temple, and [enter] the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*).
Having entered and established [the deity] by first performing the deposition of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) upon the primary liṅga, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣecayet*).
Having consecrated the *vardhanī* vessel on the pedestal and the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*) in their respective places, [one should proceed].
Having consecrated the Goddess with the water-pitcher preceded by the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa, having offered the great oblation (mahāhavir),

and having presented incense and lamps, one should proceed to the fire-sanctuary. In the Śiva-fire, [one should offer] with the head [of the mantra], using the root-mantra together with the Ghorāsana-mantra.
Having offered more than a hundred oblations and having given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should unite the fire with the Lord of the Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*).

Then, according to the method instructed by the Guru, one should unite the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*)— such as those of the *kumbha* and *vardhanī*— in their respective places, and finally, one should dismiss even Him.
Then, having gratified the deity with water-sports and other such activities, and having offered abundant sacrificial oblations, one should cause the image to undergo a ritual bath.
This is the procedure for the jar-bath (*ghaṭasnāna*).
For the purpose of suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous,
[one should perform the descent] at dawn on a holy day (*tīrthadivasa*) or during the night, preceded by the recitation of the *Brahmatāla*.
Having joined the bull standing upon the banner with the thought, "This must be performed in the most excellent manner," and having mounted the bull upon the form situated before Śiva,
one should likewise join the deities of the enclosure to their respective enclosures.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite. On that day, there is a silent offering (*maunabali*). 15. Descent (*avarohaṇa*).
Since it has been stated that "at the end of the *homa*, [there is] the portion of the oblation for the deities," one should begin the silent offering (*maunabali*) for that purpose.
The *ācārya*, having gone near Soma and Skanda, [offers] according to his capacity...

Having worshipped up to Śakti, and having performed the Daṇḍabhaṅgī and Muṇḍabhaṅgī (variant: -bhāgī), as well as the thirty-one-fold Kalānyāsa and the Śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa, one should meditate. The meditation is as follows:
I worship Guha, the Lord of the Cave, who holds the moon in his two lotus-like hands, and whose middle body is embraced by the sleeping Pārvatī, while ten million gods support his other feet.
Thus, having performed extensive worship of [the deity] together with the limbs and the five enclosures,

and having meditated upon and worshipped that goddess as will be described below, and having prayed for the welfare of the world, he— having received permission from her and observing a vow of silence— [proceeds].
Having joined his palms in *añjali*, and having placed the deities beginning with Astra— accompanied by the *anna-liṅga*— upon their vehicles, he should place the sword,
shield, weapons, and so forth, together with various forms, within his heart.

Maintaining the vow of silence while recollecting [the deity], they should, without the sound of musical instruments, take a morsel the size of a hen’s egg for the sake of a meal at the designated altars such as the *brahmasthāna*,
or at their respective locations accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, preceded by the lowering of the banner.

Having performed the *bali* offering as before and having dismissed the deities of the junctions (*sandhideva*) in their proper order, one should circumambulate [the shrine], enter the temple, descend, and place [the deity] upon the previously designated spot.
Then, one should dissolve all [the offerings], including the food-liṅga (*annaliṅga*), into water; this is the procedure for the descent (*avarohaṇavidhi*).
The procedure for the fierce festival (caṇḍotsava) of Dityavara:
thereafter, having brought the image of Caṇḍa into the sacrificial hall, with that [same] water-pot...
Having consecrated [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, having worshipped it, adorned it with the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*) and so forth,

and having offered one hundred, one thousand, or five hundred oblations into the fire as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and having dismissed that [fire], he should enter the temple (*ālaya*) accompanied by the three [arts] and the devotees.
Having circumambulated [the deity], one should install it in that place; such is the procedure for the festival of Caṇḍa. Then follows the worship of the preceptor:
one should worship the preceptor afterwards and cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
One should cause to be given gifts beginning with cattle, land, gold, and jewels, and ending with garments.
The satisfaction of the teacher’s mind; from that, Supreme Śiva is satisfied. Thus it is said.

Having honored him as well, along with the officiating priests, like Śiva, and having placed him upon a chariot or a palanquin, [the procession proceeds] with various musical instruments, dances, songs, and the like,
with the sounding of the Vedas and other scriptures, and with assemblies of devotees offering hymns of praise.
Accompanied by umbrellas, chowries, and various kinds of lamps, and together with the patron,
the preceptor, and all the people, he should circumambulate the city and enter his own home along with the vehicle; such is the procedure for the festival of the Preceptor.
Alternatively, the mounting of the chariot should be performed with the seventh [mantra]; having performed the protection ritual during the preceding night,
it should be done at dawn following the bath and consecration, at the conclusion of the daily worship.

Having performed the rites according to the rules and having worshipped in accordance with the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should perform the offerings of *caru* up to the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) as before; then, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the *Īśa* mantra, *caru* with the *Aghora* mantra, parched grain (*lāja*) with the *Hṛdaya* mantra, and sesame seeds (*tila*) with the *Vāma* mantra, and [finally] with the *Kavaca* mantra.

Having offered jaggery with the *netra* mantra and *bilva* fruit according to one's capacity, and having offered substances and grains in the northeast with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the *vyāhṛtis*, and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should restrain the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*).
Having offered protection, and having shown a full water-jar, a vessel of sesame seeds, and a cow with her calf, one should give them to the Brahmins; then,
having worshipped Vighneśa and offered sweetmeats to the deities.
After offering the milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should then mix saffron, agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, turmeric, and so forth with water in a silver vessel;
having cast into that vessel a paste of *pāṭalī*, blue lotus, jasmine, *punnāga*, *campaka*, and other such flowers.
Having surrounded the cauldron with saffron, cloth, and other materials, having placed it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of Śiva, having worshipped the cauldron with the Kāma-bīja,
and having consecrated the moist clay by worshipping it with the Mūla-mantra, one should offer incense and lamps and [worship] the Mūla-liṅga and so forth.

Having given that to the others, the preceptor himself, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should give wet mud and a turban of saffron to the patron, the attendants, and all other people; he should give them wet mud and turbans.

Thereafter, having sprinkled the chariot with the five products of the cow and with water from the *puṇyāha* ceremony, and having consecrated the chariot with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), one should place the deity upon it and, having established him there, worship all the deities within the chariot.

Having worshipped on the wheels with "Salutation to Sūrya," "Salutation to Candra," "Salutation to Hari all around," "Salutation to Vajrin," "Salutation to Ekāṅghri," and "Salutation to Dvidaṇḍaka," one should worship the Śatarudras on the banners and Dharma and the others on the limbs.

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Sadāśiva" upon the pedestal (*sthalikā*), "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti" at the joints (*sandhi*), "Salutation to Viṣṇu," "Salutation to Brahmā," and "Salutation to Skanda," [one should worship] the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) at the edges of the chariot.

Having worshipped in this sequence with the mantra "Obeisance to the serpents in the ropes," and having adorned [the area] with variegated cloths, garments, and so forth, [one should place] lion-thrones, plantain trees, and areca-nut trunks in the cardinal and intermediate directions and at the sides of the doors.
Having adorned it with clusters of plantains, coconuts, variegated cloths, and so forth,
and having appointed Brahmā as the charioteer, one should invoke the Pāśupata weapon along with its parasol, and worship the bull together with its banner.
Five-colored and greatly radiant, endowed with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting,
possessing six feet and one belly, and holding a trident and a noose, he has four arms.
Having one face and three eyes, possessing six parts and endowed with auspiciousness,
it is equipped with wheel-feet, is the support of all beings, and is mobile.
The mature region is called Sujānu; the upper region consists of the thighs.
The belly is declared to be Devāsana, and the heart is the group of pillars.
Having meditated, "The pair of Peak-shoulders (Kūṭaskandha) is proclaimed as the cause of all auspiciousness," one should worship them.
In this manner, one should worship Devī, Skanda, Vaināyaka, and Caṇḍeśvara upon their respective chariots.
Having placed [the deity] upon moist clay, having smeared it with saffron at the heart, having donned the *uṣṇīṣa* and *kavaca* [armors], having offered fruits, cakes, and so forth,
having worshipped with red flowers, and having given gifts and so on, [one honors] the preceptor and others.
Having given garments, gold, fruits, and betel leaves to the devotees and having satisfied them all,
at an auspicious moment during the favorable portion of the day and under a movable *lagna*,
he circumambulated the city preceded by benedictions and accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having helped [the deity] descend from the chariot, entered the temple, and performed the bathing preceded by the ritual ablution (*snāpana*),

one should provide the artisans and charioteers with garments and other gifts, present the great oblation (*mahāhaviḥ*), and cause it to be distributed to all; such is the procedure for mounting the chariot.
The festival of the dancing form;
the ritual for black incense;
for the sake of accomplishing desired objects.
It is the cause for obtaining excellent sons;
it destroys even the killing of a Brahmin and eradicates all enemies.
"Whoever, by the sight of the Dancing Form, enjoys the fruit [of their merit]— thereafter,

having brought the Dancing Form into the assembly pavilion, on the eighth day during the latter part of the night, having performed the protection ritual as before, [the officiant], with fruits, betel, and so forth in hand..."

Having adorned both [the images] with variegated garments and other ornaments, having offered food offerings and the like, and having circumambulated the temple, one should place them in the pavilion and pass the remainder of the night by viewing various entertainments.
On the following day, having concluded the festival, at the time of evening,

one should prepare two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity; having drawn a lotus and strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should place black aloe-wood (*kālāguru*) in the center thereof.

Having performed the worship of Vināyaka first, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having duly prepared and worshipped the *śāntikumbha* (the vessel of peace), one should perform the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and [worship] Maheśa therein.

Having performed worship, one should offer sacrificial wood, *lāja* grains, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, and so forth, each one hundred and eight times with the root mantra; then, having offered *bilva*, blue lotus, plantain, jackfruit, and the like, as well as the three sweets (*madhutraya*), one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances.
Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), bathed the deity, and adorned it,
one should place black fragrant paste upon a pedestal filled with rice, wrap it with cloth, sprinkle it with water from the *śānti* pitcher, and [fumigate it] with camphor and other substances.
Having mixed it with fragrant substances, purified it with the Astra-mantra,
enveloped it with the Varma-mantra, consecrated it with the Brahma-mantras and the limbs-mantras, worshipped it with the Mūla-mantra, and displayed the Dhenumudrā;

Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, incense, lamps, and so forth, having performed the oblation with the *sampāta* [remnants], having completed the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having dismissed the fire, one should proceed to the temple accompanied by the sounding of conchs, drums, and musical instruments.
Having circumambulated [the deity], entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), and offered [the water] to the primary liṅga (*mūlaliṅga*),

one should thereafter bathe [the deity] before Maheśa— [or, according to variant *k*: install him there]— upon the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, in the manner of the staff and the head, [making] thirty-one [offerings].

Having performed the *nyāsa* of Śrīkaṇṭha consisting of the *kalās*, [one should meditate on the Lord] who wears matted hair, the moon, and golden ornaments; who holds a *muṇḍa*, bones, the celestial river, a white *arka* flower, the supreme *mudrā*, and a peacock feather; and who is clad in a tiger skin.
Clad in a garment of action,
with his right hand extending the *abhaya* mudrā and a *ḍamaru* drum,
and the other [left hand] extended.
Holding fire in his left hand, he stands upon the back of a serpent that is lying prostrate.
Having made his right foot adamantine and lifting up his left foot—
which possesses sandals shimmering with a central banner, small bells, jewels,
and anklets; and which has a crocodile-shaped earring on the right ear-lobe and a lotus-leaf ornament on the left—
I bow to Naṭeśa Śiva, smeared with ashes, joined by Umā, and possessing three eyes.
Having meditated thus,
[one visualizes] Śyāmā, with two eyes, two arms, in the *tribhaṅga* posture, with her right foot placed forward and slightly bent.
The Supreme Goddess should have her left hand adorned with a lotus and a bracelet, while her right hand is extended in a supporting gesture.
Having thus honored both [deities] and offered incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should offer] milk-rice (*pāyasa*) made with flour (*paiṣṭya*), as well as fruits, cakes, and the like.
Having offered the betel-leaf together with [other items] and given it, one should apply a black fragrant ointment;

this should be done on the forehead with the Aghora mantra, on the crest-lock with the Śikhā mantra, and on both arms everywhere with the Sadyojāta mantra, or one may cause it to be given in all places with the Sadyojāta mantra.

Thereafter, one should cause [the substances] to be offered upon the foreheads and necks of the images of Sadāśiva and the other deities; for female images, one should fix them with the root mantra at the heart.
Afterwards, the preceptor, together with the image-makers, should hold [the deity] and cause it to be given to all the practitioners and devotees;
[he should place] the God upon a jeweled throne, Gaurī to his left, and [Śiva] to his right.
Having caused [the image] to be mounted together with the preceptor, the king— accompanied by dancers, female dancers, and mardakas on both sides,
and having performed song and dance along with instrumental music— should dance until the completion of the seven planetary positions.

Having entered the inner sanctum (ālaya), one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā) and other rites as before. Afterwards, having placed [the deity] in the assembly hall (āsthānamaṇṭapa), one should offer the eight-limbed prostration (sāṣṭāṅga), present the water for honor (arghya), and offer fruit.
One should worship with the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) and other rites.
