Afterwards, having bathed [the deity] with the products of the cow (*gavya*) and so forth, and having established [it], one should consecrate pure camphor as before.

Having taken up all the ritual implements beginning with the plowshare, having adorned [the deity] with very white jasmine flowers and white garments, having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and having presented incense and lamps,
at the time of departure, the procession should be conducted slowly.

There, with recitation, dance, song, and so forth, having arranged a procession as before at the front of the city gate or atop the flagstaff, and having performed all rites such as the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) as before, one should enter the temple,
worship with all ritual offerings, and spend the remainder of the night.
One should dispel [the obstacles] by beholding diversions.
At sunrise, having worshipped and adorned the Lord of Dance (Nṛteśa) on a riverbank or similar location, (p. 36) [one should proceed].

As before, having performed the ritual ablution (*tīrtha*), having released the protective thread (*kautuka*), and having circumambulated the city and other sites, one should, in a pure location, cause [the king] to hear the subjugation of the wicked, the protection of the virtuous, and the proclamation of all legal procedures, as well as the amorous quarrel of the Goddess.
Having removed the outer covering and entered the inner sanctum, one should establish [the deity] in its own place;
having worshipped it and consecrated it with ablutions and other rites,
one should perform the pure dance— this is the ritual for black fragrances.
17. Regarding the marriage ceremony:

subsequently, on the tenth, seventh, or fifth day, one should cause the marriage to be performed according to the rules and hold a festive rite for the auspicious vow (*kalyāṇavrata*) with ceremonial honors.
k: 46) The Procedure for the Festival of the Goddess:
One should perform the festival for nine days, seven days, three days, or one day.

On the night of the eleventh day, having adorned everything beginning with Indra’s celestial chariot (*vimāna*), having sprinkled it with consecrated water, and having first bathed and then adorned the deity,
he placed all the gods upon their respective celestial chariots.

At the time of the circumambulation of the city, having adorned the northeast direction with a water-shed (*prapā*), flowers, banners, and so forth, and having brought Śiva seated upon his celestial chariot (*vimāna*) into its center—
preceded by the Goddess and ending with Caṇḍeśa— the king, together with the sacrificer and musical instruments, [should proceed].

Having performed three circumambulations, at the time of entering the inner sanctum (layapraveśa), one should arrange for the dispelling of any affectionate quarrels and the display of diversions at the front of the gatehouse or atop the palace; then, one should cause the deity to enter according to the prescribed rite— this is the ritual procedure for the festival of the Goddess.
18. The Ritual for the Festival of the Devotee’s Image.

Now, having established the devotee’s image and others either before Śiva or in a pavilion, and having performed their ablution preceded by a ceremonial bath, one should consecrate and adorn both the mobile and immobile images.

Having performed the full festival as before, and having placed [the offerings] before the clay icons, one should cause the consecrated disciples, practitioners, and devotees to receive the powder, and bestow upon them saffron turbans, sacred threads, garlands, and so forth.
Having praised [the Lord] with the hymns of the devotees, having given betel leaves and other offerings to the devotees of Śiva,

and having circumambulated the city, one enters the temple; then, having stationed everyone in their respective places, having offered the oblation, and having presented incense and lamps, [one gives] clothing and other gifts to those who know how to sing the praises of Śiva.
"One should cause [the gifts] to be given"—this is the procedure for the festival of the consecrated food (bhaktotsava).
The pacification of the festival (utsavaśānti):
on the following day, preceded by the great ablution (mahāsnāna), there is the fire-offering for peace (śāntihoma) and the fire-offering for the image (mūrtihoma).
Having performed the directional fire-offerings (*diśā-homa*) and so forth in sequence, and having conferred the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should cause the removal of fatigue;
this constitutes the fivefold ritual activity of the festival (*utsava-pañcaka-kṛtya*).
Festivity is said to be fivefold, consisting of persistence, emergence, and dissolution,
as well as concealment and grace; thus it comprises the fivefold activity beginning with emanation.
The auspicious rite of planting the sprout, the hoisting of the banner,
and the binding of the protective thread— these are declared to be the rites of creation (*sṛṣṭikarman*).

That which is joined with the festival of the vehicle (*vāhana*), the performance of *homa*, and the movement of offerings (*bali*), is declared to be the rite of maintenance (*sthitikarma*); now the rite of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is being described.
The application of nocturnal powders, the mounting of chariots,
and likewise the festival of black aloe-wood are well-known in the Āgamas.
48) [The states of] silence, festival, concealment, the journey of power, and grace;
at the beginning and end of the day of the sacred site (tīrtha), there is affection, strife, and celebration.
"The fivefold act, beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*), is joined to the seed and the field.
Thus ends [the section on] the festival of Vaināyaka and so forth, in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, who is also known by the name Parameśvara.
The ritual procedure for the festival of devotees (concluding with the festival of devotees) is completed.
[Now follows] the ritual procedure for the monthly festival and the ritual procedure for the auspicious times.
The transition of the moment is subtle and difficult to perceive even for those with discerning vision;
through its conjunction, the thirty channels below and above are purified.
O twice-born Haras, it has been declared that there will be thirty meritorious nāḍīs in the southern course, while in the northern [course] they have passed away.
The transits, the equinoxes, and especially the two solstices—
occur in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo in the southern [solstice].

O twice-born ones, this is called Viṣṇupada, which yields fruit exceeding that of the equinoxes. When the sun’s transit occurs in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, or Sagittarius, these are declared to be the "Sixty-four Gates" (Ṣaḍaśītimukha), which are the most meritorious of all.
Sixteen *nāḍīs* are before the solar transit and sixteen after it;
in the current [transit] of Libra and Aries, however, there are ten *nāḍīs* on both sides.
It occurs when Viṣṇu is in his northern course, likewise during the period of Viṣuva,
at the mouth of the Ṣaḍaśīti, and indeed when the southern solstice has passed.

Bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts should be performed at night during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the transition of the sun between zodiac signs, at weddings, after a calamity, on auspicious occasions of increase, and during optional religious observances.
One should perform a festival for the deity and worship Śiva right there;
whatever channels (nāḍīs) are present there, they are all considered most meritorious.

Then, at the time of the transit (*saṅkrānti*), having bathed the deity as before preceded by the ritual ablution (*snāna*) and other rites, and having adorned the primary *liṅga* and other objects with all ornaments, [one should worship] the images of the devotees such as Vināyaka, Soma, Skanda, and others, accompanied by [all] the [attendant] deities.
Having led the procession clockwise around the village, the city, or the residence,
one should first perform the *nīrājana* and other rites at the site of Brahmā or in front of the bull, and then install [the deity] in its own place.
Thus, when this is performed within the kingdom, no fault regarding the month occurs;
therefore, one should properly celebrate the festival with every possible effort.
Thus concludes the ritual for the monthly festival. Now, regarding the ritual for the fortnightly festival,
there is the new-moon festival.
In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes diminished;
or indeed, in the eighth part of the new moon day, it becomes minute once again.

Sinīvālī is considered to be that [new moon] when the moon is visible, while Kuhū is considered to be that when the moon has disappeared. When it occurs at midday or later, it proceeds as the subsequent [lunar day], the Amāvāsyā.
But that [Amāvāsyā] pierced by the Bhūta (the fourteenth tithi) is to be known as such;
it would not be the fifteenth [tithi] if there is not even a single ghaṭikā of Amāvāsyā remaining at the beginning of the Pratipad.
Even if pierced by the Bhūta-tithi (the fourteenth day), it should be employed for rites pertaining to the gods and ancestors,
provided that the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) overlaps with the new moon (amāvāsyā) during the forenoon.
In rites for the gods, that [lunar day] should always be treated as if it were pierced by the asterism when [the sun is] in Libra,
Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, or Gemini.
Even if the new moon day is pierced by the lunar mansion Bhūtā, it should be honored with effort.

On this occasion, the fourteenth day is complete, leading toward the inexhaustible Nandā and other [lunar days]. One should perform the festival for the deity on the fourteenth (bhūtā), and perform the pilgrimage at the sacred site on the new moon (amā).
The new moon day on a Monday, the seventh lunar day on a Sunday,
and the fourth lunar day on a Tuesday yield fruit equal to that of the equinoxes.
If it falls on a Monday during the new moon, it shall indeed be equal to Śivarātri;
one should perform a night vigil and then carry out a festival for the deity.
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) falls on a Monday in conjunction with the Ardra asterism, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices, austerities, and gifts by fasting on that occasion.
Then, on the new moon day, having performed the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) preceded by the five products of the cow for the root-liṅga and other images to be installed and removed,
and having adorned them with all ornaments and offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), [one should proceed].

In a village, market town, or similar location, having led the deity in circumambulation— without the taking of offerings (*bali*) or wandering, but accompanied by parasols, chowries, and so forth, together with many various lamps and various musical instruments— *Note: The bracketed terms (*k*) refer to variant readings found in the manuscript.*
Having brought [the deity] to the station of Brahmā and having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) and other rites as before, one should establish it in its own place.
Thus, the mortal who causes this to be done shall attain a meritorious state.
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring a daughter obtains an auspicious daughter.
One who seeks wealth shall obtain abundant riches; one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation. The rain-god shall not fail to rain at the proper time, and there shall be no disease or calamity.
"By the festival of the new moon alone, one shall obtain all desires"—
thus concludes the ritual procedure for the new moon festival.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the full moon festival.
Rākā and Anumatī are considered to be the two forms of the full moon;
that which is the earlier full moon is Anumatī, and that which follows is Rākā.
The end of the fortnight, known as the fifteenth day, is remembered as the full moon (paurṇamāsī);
it is desired on the sixteenth day, while the intermediate [day] is on the fifteenth day.

The fourteenth day is considered inferior and inauspicious on the seventeenth day [of the lunar fortnight]. All days beginning from the first (pratipad) until the sun rises again are renowned as "complete" for pure rites dedicated to the gods.

The second, third, fifth, sixth, eighth, ninth, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days are joined respectively with the pairs [of deities]: Yuga, Agni, Yama, Bhūta, Ṣaṇmanu, Vasu, Randhra, Rudra, and Pūrṇimā.
Even if the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is pierced by the previous lunar day, the pair of days yields great fruit;
even then, one should first perform the worship of Vighneśa, beginning with the offerings and ending with the food oblation (naivedya).

Having performed the ritual action, one should lead the deities, such as Vighneśa, adorned with all ornaments, on a circumambulation of the city and other sites, and then install them in their respective places as before;
by this entire procedure according to the rules, any defect of omission shall be destroyed.
"By the command of Śiva"— thus concludes the procedure for the Full Moon Festival.
Next is the procedure for the Constellation Festival.
Wherever one might lead the sun to its setting by means of speech, there alone one should observe the lunar mansion with the moon— except for the asterism Śravaṇa.
Until sunset and for three muhūrtas thereafter,
one should remain right there; on that day, one should perform bathing and worship as long as the lunar mansion is reached before half a watch has passed.
One should perform that lunar mansion vow; in some cases, the breaking of the fast occurs at sunrise.
By worshipping Śiva under the asterism Kṛttikā, a human being attains happiness;
one desiring offspring shall obtain them under Rohiṇī, and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), he shall become endowed with vigor.
In Ārdrā, one obtains all prosperity; in Punarvasu, from the Kṣatriyas;
in Puṣya, nourishment; and by worshipping Hara in Āśleṣā, one obtains excellent sons.
Pūrvaphalgunī brings good fortune characterized by a mouth full of one's own kinsmen;
and under Uttarā-phalgunī, one becomes disposed toward giving.
One who worships Hara in his hand attains preeminence among the virtuous;
likewise, one obtains a beautiful wife who captivates the minds of all.
Svātī bestows profit from trade; under Viśākhā, one has many desires;
and for those performing [rites] under Anurādhā, it shall grant the turning of the wheel.
In Jyeṣṭhā, there is the attainment of great wealth; in Mūla, excellent health;
in the first Āṣāḍhā, the acquisition of fame; and in the Uttarāṣāḍhās, the increase of renown.
Under Śravaṇā one obtains pleasant enjoyments; under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth;
under Abhijit, one becomes a knower of the Vedas; and under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), success as a physician.
One should obtain goats and sheep under Proṣṭhapadā, and cattle under its successor;
one should take away gold under Revatī, and horses under Aśvinī.
The worshipper obtains, at each respective [constellation], excellent longevity under Bharaṇī;
therefore, with every effort, one should hold a festival during these constellations.
Fasting on the day of Ārdrā yields merit multiplied by ten million times ten million;
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of millions of other sacrifices.
Whether he be a Samayin, a Putraka, or a Sādhaka initiated by Hara, he obtains the fruit of giving ten million maidens in marriage to Śaṅkara.
He who does not observe the Śarvarṣa [observance] shall go to hell as a sinner;
this applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
Śūdras, and men of intermediate castes.
Whether she be a maiden, a widow, a woman of gentle mind, or one observing the vow of an ascetic;
O best of the twice-born, whether one has been initiated or not, for each constellation,
one should perform worship at night, as well as eating, bathing, and giving gifts there.
Having beheld the God of gods, and having offered praise and prostration,
one should provide for the Brahmins according to one's ability with gold coverings and meals.
Then, following the evening worship, having worshipped all the deities according to the prescribed rites with as much elaboration as one’s means allow— excluding the ghee-bath—
and having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), [one should offer] the *somāskanda* [oblation], the parasol, the fly-whisk, and so forth.
Having circumambulated the city or the temple accompanied by many various lamps, and having performed the *nīrājana* and other rites as before, he should cause [the deity] to enter the temple.
The mortal who causes this to be done thus is indeed Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
His portents vanish, as do the terrible afflictions caused by malevolent planets.
Freed from all diseases, he prospers in long life and happiness;
O Brahmins, in a single year, he certainly obtains a virtuous son.
The Festival of the Days: On Sunday, when the Raudra [muhūrta] occurs, there is supreme health;
on Monday, it bestows happiness; on Tuesday, it grants victory in battle.
On Wednesday, all desires are fulfilled; on Thursday, knowledge along with the sciences is attained;
on Friday, great wealth is gained; and on Saturday, the destruction of untimely death occurs.
Having understood this, one should worship Śiva there with diligent effort.
Thus ends the procedure beginning with the Brahmattāla and concluding with the Ṛkṣotsava, in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose name is Parameśvara.
The ritual for the Great [Deity] is completed.
